analysis.one_liner: Lets workers refuse forced arbitration and keeps it out of job contracts.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a single cosponsor and died in a House Judiciary subcommittee without a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change federal arbitration law so that an employer could not force a worker to sign away the right to go to court as a condition of getting or keeping a job. After a dispute arose, arbitration could happen only if both sides agreed in writing. It died in committee without a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers, especially new hires and low-wage employees, who today routinely sign pre-dispute arbitration clauses as a condition of employment. The bill would let them decline arbitration and take an employment dispute to court instead [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits an employer from requiring an employee to arbitrate a dispute as a condition of employment [S2][S3].
Allows arbitration only if one party requests it in writing after a dispute arises and the other consents in writing within 60 days [S2][S3].
Applies to employment contracts entered into or modified after enactment [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers who rely on mandatory arbitration clauses would lose a tool that keeps disputes out of court, where jury awards and discovery are typically costlier and more public. The commercial arbitration industry would lose a large, guaranteed stream of employment cases.

drawbacks.text: Employers argue that arbitration is faster and cheaper for resolving disputes, and that a blanket ban on pre-dispute clauses removes a useful option some workers and unions might prefer [S2].
Because it reaches employment contracts under federal arbitration law, the bill would override existing contract terms going forward, a significant change to established employment practice [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers, the benefit is substantial: it restores access to the courts, with public proceedings and juries, for job discrimination, wage, and wrongful-treatment disputes. The cost falls on employers in the form of costlier, slower, and more public litigation, and on arbitration providers who lose caseload. The bill offers no compromise mechanism beyond mutual post-dispute agreement, which is its central design choice rather than a flaw.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and then to a subcommittee, where it sat until the Congress ended with no hearing and no vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Robert Andrews introduced the bill on March 1, 2001, and it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the same day [S1][S5].
On March 9, 2001, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Commercial and Administrative Law, where no further action was taken [S5].
No member of the House cosponsored the bill [S4].
The bill never reached the House floor, and the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003, without it advancing [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that use mandatory arbitration clauses kept a system that routes employment disputes into private arbitration, and the commercial arbitration industry kept the caseload, because the bill never advanced.

for.name: Rep. Robert E. Andrews
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill; no colleague joined him as a cosponsor

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Never reported the bill out of committee or scheduled it for consideration

against.name: Subcommittee on Commercial and Administrative Law
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on March 9, 2001, and took no further action on it for the rest of the Congress

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no member cosponsored the bill, so the partisan shape of support and opposition never showed itself; the sponsor was a Democrat.

industries.note: Mandatory arbitration clauses let employers resolve discrimination, wage, and firing disputes in private proceedings without juries, at far lower cost than court. The bill would bar conditioning employment on signing such a clause, so the industry's savings run directly against workers' access to the courts [S2][S3].

Arbitration firms and their arbitrators are paid per case, and employment disputes are a major source of that caseload. Banning forced pre-dispute arbitration clauses would shrink that revenue stream.
Workers regained access to court would mean more employment cases litigated publicly, work that arbitration clauses currently divert to private arbitrators.
